Incumbent Democratic Mayor Michael Nutter could not run for re-election to a third consecutive term due to the home-rule charter's two-term limit. Registered Democrats hold a formidable 7-to-1 ratio over registered Republicans in Philadelphia, giving Democratic candidates a distinct advantage in citywide elections. The mayoral primary elections were held on May 19, 2015. Kenney won the primary in a landslide with 55.83% of the vote, defeating a crowded field of five other Democratic candidates, including [Anthony H. Williams](/wiki/Anthony_H._Williams "Anthony H. Williams") and former District Attorney [Lynn Abraham](/wiki/Lynn_Abraham "Lynn Abraham"). Republican [Melissa Murray Bailey](/wiki/Melissa_Murray_Bailey "Melissa Murray Bailey"), a business executive, ran unopposed for the [Republican](/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") nomination. Kenney won with 85.1% of the vote.[[12]](#cite_note-12) Kenney was inaugurated as the 99th Mayor of Philadelphia on January 4, 2016.

Kenney was reelected as mayor in 2019. The Democratic primary was held on May 21, 2019, and he defeated former [City Controller](/wiki/City_Controller "City Controller") [Alan Butkovitz](/wiki/Alan_Butkovitz "Alan Butkovitz") and [Pennsylvania State Senator](/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_Senate "Pennsylvania State Senate") [Anthony Hardy Williams](/wiki/Anthony_Hardy_Williams "Anthony Hardy Williams") with 67% of the vote.[[13]](#cite_note-13) On November 5, 2019, Kenney won re-election by defeating [Billy Ciancaglini](/wiki/Billy_Ciancaglini "Billy Ciancaglini"), a Philadelphia defense attorney and fellow La Salle grad, in the general election[[14]](#cite_note-14) with more than 80% of the vote.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

fanoutqa_002049.t: Breast cancer :: Health disparities in breast cancer :: chunk_0028
fanoutqa_002049.x:
Breast cancer :: Health disparities in breast cancer :: chunk_0028
There are ethnic disparities in the [mortality rates](/wiki/Mortality_rate "Mortality rate") for breast cancer as well as in breast cancer treatment. Breast cancer is the most prevalent cancer affecting women of every ethnic group in the United States. Breast cancer incidence among Black women aged 45 and older is higher than that of white women in the same age group. White women aged 60–84 have higher incidence rates of breast cancer than Black women. Despite this, Black women at every age are more likely to die of breast cancer.[[187]](#cite_note-Health_and_Racial_Disparity_in_Brea-187)

Breast cancer treatment has improved greatly over the years; however, Black women are still less likely to obtain treatment compared to white women.[[187]](#cite_note-Health_and_Racial_Disparity_in_Brea-187) Risk factors such as [socioeconomic status](/wiki/Socioeconomic_status "Socioeconomic status"), late-stage, or breast cancer at diagnosis, genetic differences in tumor subtypes, and differences in healthcare access all contribute to these disparities. Socioeconomic determinants affecting the disparity in breast cancer illness include poverty, [culture](/wiki/Cultural_differences_in_breast_cancer_diagnosis_and_treatment "Cultural differences in breast cancer diagnosis and treatment"), and social injustice. In Hispanic women, the incidence of breast cancer is lower than in non-Hispanic women, but it is often diagnosed at a later stage than in white women with larger tumors.

Black women are usually diagnosed with breast cancer at a younger age than white women. The median age of diagnosis for Black women is 59, in comparison to 62 in White women. The incidence of breast cancer in Black women has increased by 0.4% per year since 1975, and 1.5% per year among Asian/Pacific Islander women since 1992. Incidence rates were stable for non-Hispanic White, Hispanic, and Native American women. The five-year survival rate is noted to be 81% in Black women and 92% in White women. Chinese and Japanese women have the highest survival rates.[[187]](#cite_note-Health_and_Racial_Disparity_in_Brea-187)

On March 18, 2013, Fitzpatrick signed a two-year contract with the [Tennessee Titans](/wiki/Tennessee_Titans "Tennessee Titans").[[54]](#cite_note-54)

During a Week 4 38–13 victory over the [New York Jets](/wiki/2013_New_York_Jets_season "2013 New York Jets season"), Fitzpatrick made his Titans debut, replacing an injured [Jake Locker](/wiki/Jake_Locker "Jake Locker") in the third quarter. Fitzpatrick completed three of eight passes for 108 yards and a 77-yard touchdown pass to [Nate Washington](/wiki/Nate_Washington "Nate Washington").[[55]](#cite_note-55)

Fitzpatrick played in 11 games and started in nine of them. He finished the season with a 3–6 record as the starting quarterback, beating division rivals [Jacksonville Jaguars](/wiki/2013_Jacksonville_Jaguars_season "2013 Jacksonville Jaguars season") and [Houston Texans](/wiki/2013_Houston_Texans_season "2013 Houston Texans season") in the final two games of the season. Fitzpatrick completed the season throwing for 2,454 yards, 14 touchdowns, and 12 interceptions to go along with 43 carries for 225 yards and three touchdowns.[[56]](#cite_note-56)

Fitzpatrick was released on March 14, 2014, and replaced by [Charlie Whitehurst](/wiki/Charlie_Whitehurst "Charlie Whitehurst").[[57]](#cite_note-57)

Nouvelle-Aquitaine comprises twelve [departments](/wiki/Departments_of_France "Departments of France"): [Charente](/wiki/Charente "Charente"), [Charente-Maritime](/wiki/Charente-Maritime "Charente-Maritime"), [Corrèze](/wiki/Corr%C3%A8ze "Corrèze"), [Creuse](/wiki/Creuse "Creuse"), [Dordogne](/wiki/Dordogne "Dordogne"), [Gironde](/wiki/Gironde "Gironde"), [Landes](/wiki/Landes_(department) "Landes (department)"), [Lot-et-Garonne](/wiki/Lot-et-Garonne "Lot-et-Garonne"), [Pyrénées-Atlantiques](/wiki/Pyr%C3%A9n%C3%A9es-Atlantiques "Pyrénées-Atlantiques"), [Deux-Sèvres](/wiki/Deux-S%C3%A8vres "Deux-Sèvres"), [Vienne](/wiki/Vienne_(department) "Vienne (department)") and [Haute-Vienne](/wiki/Haute-Vienne "Haute-Vienne").

During the University Council meeting held in [Yishan](/wiki/Yizhou_District,_Hechi "Yizhou District, Hechi"), [Guangxi](/wiki/Guangxi "Guangxi") on 19 November 1938, "seeking truth" ([Chinese](/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"): 求是; [pinyin](/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Qiúshì*) was made the motto of the university, upon President Chu Kochen's advice. Qiushi is an excerpt of the famous quote in [Yangmingism](/wiki/Yangmingism "Yangmingism"), "A [Gentleman](/wiki/Junzi "Junzi") learns only to know what is right. ([Chinese](/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"): 君子之學，唯求其是)" It was made the name of the former body Qiushi Academy in 1897, which means seeking truth and has the same pronunciation as truth in English. According to Chu,

> Seeking truth is not limited to studying hard or doing experiments in the lab. As [Doctrine of the Mean](/wiki/Doctrine_of_the_Mean "Doctrine of the Mean") says, seeking truth is 'to study extensively, inquire prudently, think carefully, distinguish clearly, and practice earnestly.'

In May 1988, "pursuing innovation" was added to the university motto by the university council, to adapt the motto to the times of the [reform and opening up](/wiki/Reform_and_opening_up "Reform and opening up"). President [Lu Yongxiang](/wiki/Lu_Yongxiang_(engineer) "Lu Yongxiang (engineer)") explained in 1992,

> Strictly speaking, pursuing innovation is included in seeking truth, [...] but people often regard seeking truth as being practical, emphasising the acknowledgement and application of the existing body of knowledge and the objective analysis and knowledge of the reality, with no emphasis on being creative and innovative.
